entries.organization: Duke University × Top-Tier Foundation Model Company
entries.summary: Co-developed quality control for more than 300 contributors across travel, food delivery, consumer goods, and e-commerce advertising. Built reliability-based review rules, expert adjudication, and random audits; audit records showed a higher share of outputs meeting every user requirement under the combined process. Extended this work into a mathematical design connecting residual-corrected quality estimation, audit allocation, and reviewer capacity. In a 10,000-submission synthetic experiment with ideal residual calibration, the allocation reduced estimation variance by 17.79% versus uniform sampling at equal expected audit cost.
entries.detailTitle: Scalable Expert Quality Control and Adaptive Review
keyContributions: Designed adaptive review rules using Beta-Binomial posteriors, credible intervals, verified sample counts, and task risk. In one advertising workflow, flagged outputs received three additional reviewers and initially accepted outputs received one or two; expert adjudications updated contributor records, feedback, and review intensity.

Combined independent random audits with targeted review and turned recurring disagreements into clearer acceptance standards. Distinguished missing information, ambiguous criteria, and defective submissions; revised instructions, boundary cases, and expert calibration. Compared reviewer-error models and cost-sensitive routing methods to inform review and escalation rules.

Used SQL and Python to connect task, review, acceptance, time, and behavioral records, reconciling platform activity with Hubstaff to guide staffing and workload decisions. Turned client-reported defects into engineering investigation records and delivered operating guidance linking review, adjudication, feedback, and standards revision.

Compared approximately 20 curated hotels with more than 100 eligible options using logistic regression with decision-stage interactions, dwell-time transformations, and distributional analysis. The broader choice set increased browsing time more clearly than clicks, informing recommendations for the exploratory settings tested.

Extended the production procedures into a joint mathematical design for residual-corrected quality estimation, audit allocation, and reviewer capacity. Derived allocation rules from residual uncertainty and verification cost, separating error risk, audit information value, and the loss additional review can remove.

Validated the allocation mechanism in a synthetic batch of 10,000 submissions. With ideal residual calibration and equal expected audit cost, the design reduced estimation variance by 17.79% versus uniform allocation. Used 200,000 independent sampling repetitions to check the analytical variances.

entries.organization: Duke University × Top-Tier Foundation Model Company
entries.summary: Led financial and business task design for a frontier foundation model company, defining the task environment, reference cases, synthetic expansion rules, and expert preference protocols for post-training and evaluation. Guided experts with doctoral-level subject expertise and created Batch Zero to test independent execution before scaling; the company adopted it for other new tasks. The accompanying analysis derives constraint-preserving generation methods and quantifies how input changes, future information, and related task variants affect labels and evaluation.
entries.detailTitle: Financial Task Design and Synthetic Data Engineering
keyContributions: Defined the task environment and scenario matrix for financial and business decisions, specifying capabilities, evidence, inputs, decisive variables, and acceptance conditions. Led golden-case development with complete reference answers, reasoning, and scoring criteria, guiding experts with doctoral-level subject expertise through task construction.

Selected synthetic expansion methods around the relationships each task had to preserve. Used copulas and conditional sampling for joint company indicators, and CTGAN and TabDDPM for mixed numerical and categorical records. Applied constrained sampling and variable transformations to maintain ranges, temporal ordering, and calculated relationships.

Developed dynamic paths using stochastic differential equations and neural SDEs, specifying dependence and volatility around task requirements. Used Brownian bridges and stochastic interpolation for known intermediate observations or endpoints, matching each construction to the information available in the task.

Designed diagnostic cases and a five-level pairwise preference protocol linking judgments to evidence, decisive variables, and rules. Managed expanded inputs, reference solutions, and labels as linked objects: rechecked business relationships after input changes, generated fresh model responses, and commissioned new expert comparisons.

Created Batch Zero to test independent execution before scaling, using pilot findings to revise instructions, cases, and expert calibration. Set Batch One entry conditions and handed off validated cases, expansion rules, and review procedures while retaining task-design responsibility. The company subsequently adopted Batch Zero for other new tasks.

In the accompanying research, derived exact Gaussian sampling under affine constraints; 200,000 synthetic draws in 12 dimensions with four constraints achieved a maximum residual of 1.21 × 10⁻¹⁴. Derived label-stability conditions and quantified how future information and correlated task variants affect evaluation precision and production cost.

entries.organization: Duke University × Top-Tier AI Research Lab
entries.summary: Developed original physics, mathematics, and risk-engineering tasks, complete solutions, and failure feedback for a frontier AI research laboratory. Built acceptance methods around explicit proof requirements and valid alternative solutions. The accompanying analysis develops proof obligations, error certificates, and controlled task transformations. In an exact-arithmetic stress test of 3,600 constructed submissions across 600 quadratic problem families, semantic certificate checking accepted all 1,200 valid submissions and rejected all 2,400 invalid ones, while retaining alternative proofs that strict reference-path matching rejected.
entries.detailTitle: Scientific Reasoning Evaluation and Task Design
keyContributions: Translated physics, mathematics, and risk engineering into explicit capability specifications and original problems. Verified complete reference solutions during task acceptance, requiring justified modeling choices, decisive transformations, and supported conclusions. Checked physical models, formula applicability, computation, approximations, and limits separately.

Established acceptance standards that accommodate valid alternative methods. Classified missing conditions, incorrect models, formula misuse, calculation errors, and proof gaps; identified unsupported steps and corrective feedback. Compared symbolic computation, numerical verification, formal proof, and expert judgment to determine the evidence each argument required.

Designed diagnostic variants using invariants, boundary conditions, assumption changes, and distractors. Compared item response theory, multidimensional ability models, and representative item selection to study difficulty and model discrimination. The accompanying analysis derives how controlled task transformations carry optimality tolerances into the transformed problem.

Used path invariance of vertical travel time to reduce an original kinematics task to horizontal scheduling. Proved an attained minimum completion time and an unattained supremum, and derived harmonic-number asymptotics for staircase paths approaching the upper bound. Incorporated feasibility, optimality, and attainment into the reference solution.

Formalized acceptance through proof obligations and error certificates in the accompanying research. Derived a projected-residual bound on the optimality gap for equality-constrained strongly convex quadratic problems, linking certificates to solution quality. Derived grading-error effects on model comparisons and supervision signals, and analyzed task-family dependence and expert-review cost.

Tested 3,600 constructed submissions across 600 quadratic families using exact arithmetic. Certificate checks accepted all 1,200 valid submissions and rejected all 2,400 invalid ones. Answer-only checking accepted 75% of invalid submissions; strict reference-path matching rejected 50% of valid submissions, demonstrating the value of checking proof obligations.

entries.organization: Duke University × Leading Global Alternative Asset Manager
entries.summary: Developed an investment-research workflow that carried corrections to company evidence through scores, predictions, rankings, and explanations in a university-industry collaboration. Combined structured scoring, AI-assisted verification, tree models, SHAP, and stability analysis to make conclusions traceable and repeatable. The accompanying mathematical analysis represents evidence uncertainty and model choice jointly, derives conditions for certifying company comparisons, and prioritizes verification by the decision regret a query can remove. Constructed examples show how shared errors cancel and targeted verification resolves uncertain rankings.
entries.detailTitle: AI-Driven Investment Research and Explainable Risk Analysis
keyContributions: Converted operating, financial, sustainability, questionnaire, and third-party materials into structured scoring rules with traceable evidence. Directed AI-assisted verification toward unsupported claims and cross-source contradictions, then mapped findings to scoring inputs and company assessments requiring revision.

Built a repeatable reassessment procedure: correct affected records, recompute scores and predictions, and trace changes in values, rankings, and feature contributions. Distinguished rule-based scores, learned predictions, and model explanations to locate discrepancies in evidence, measurement rules, or modeling and document the conclusions supported after correction.

Used tree models to study nonlinearities, thresholds, and interactions, and SHAP to explain feature contributions relative to a prediction baseline. Connected explanations to company materials and industry context to identify diligence questions. Compared tabular deep learning and pretrained models in the methodological research.

Ran sensitivity analysis and bootstrap resampling to assess changes in company scores and industry findings across samples and assumptions. In methodological research, compared conditional attribution, feature grouping, and explanations across Rashomon sets to examine feature dependence and consistency among similarly performing models.

In the accompanying analysis, developed a joint uncertainty framework combining unresolved company evidence with alternative models supported by validation data. Derived conditions for certifying score or prediction orderings across that set. In a constructed comparison, joint modeling preserved a 0.6-point difference obscured by separate company intervals.

Derived a verification criterion based on the worst-case decision regret a query can remove. In a constructed eight-scenario comparison, one targeted query reduced worst-case regret from 0.61 score units to zero, connecting evidence dependence, model uncertainty, and verification cost to the next research decision.
notes: The university-industry partner was a leading global alternative asset manager with more than $300 billion in assets under management as of June 2026.

entries.detailTitle: China Market Entry for a Premium European Appliance Brand

entries.summary: Applied statistical methods to sustainability assessment and green-credit screening within China Construction Bank's internal framework. entries.detailTitle: PCA-Based Sustainability Analysis and Green-Credit Screening
keyContributions: Analyzed financial, operational, and environmental data for approximately 2,000 entities within CCB's framework of more than 30 indicators, assessing overall scores alongside minimum requirements for individual metrics.

Used PCA to identify overlapping indicator information and construct compact representations for candidate comparison. Incorporated life cycle assessment principles into sustainability analysis, examining operating and environmental factors alongside financial performance.

Delivered a methodology note explaining scoring logic, data sources, model behavior, and edge cases to product managers and risk officers assessing the method for platform use.

entries.organization: Autonomous Authority in Space: Risk Tradeoffs and the Law of Delegation
entries.summary: Developed a legal framework for authorizing autonomous space operations when delayed human intervention creates risks of its own. Formulated a two-threshold test separating the authority to act from the evidence needed to delegate execution. Applied it to delayed spacecraft operations, orbital avoidance, debris capture, and SETI, then proposed task-specific authorization records. The resulting framework identifies which decisions can be authorized in advance, which require renewed review, and what evidence must support each choice.
entries.detailTitle: Autonomous Authority in Space: Risk Tradeoffs and the Law of Delegation
keyContributions: Specified a decision procedure linking legal authority, evidence for delegation, and the time at which human review can still change the outcome. Distinguished individual approval, advance-constrained action, and fallback behavior as separate supervisory choices.

Designed an authorization record specifying responsible actors, permitted actions, operating conditions, exposed interests, and reassessment triggers. Connected these terms to independent scrutiny and event records that allow consequential decisions to be reconstructed.

Compared delayed spacecraft operations and orbital avoidance against existing automation and ground review. Analyzed how latency, uncertain trajectories, simultaneous maneuvers, and failed coordination affect delegation and redistribute risk among operators.

Used debris capture and SETI to distinguish technical capability from permission to affect another party's interests or confirm a scientific interpretation. Proposed scientific verification through alternative explanations, independent observations, and documented evidence.

Integrated review delays, compliance costs, disclosure risks, and correlated failures into the proposed controls. Developed proportionate reassessment around material changes, reusable evidence, and legally competent institutions, making the burdens of supervision part of the authorization decision.

entries.organization: Small States and the Governance of Strategic Space Dependence
entries.summary: Developed a comparative legal framework for assessing small states' control over foreign-dependent space infrastructure. Analyzed New Zealand's launch regulation, Norway's Arctic satellite partnership, and Luxembourg's LUXEOSys procurement to distinguish permission, ownership, operational rights, and implementation capacity. Proposed an accountable-acceptance standard for strategic dependencies, linking interruption powers and response rights to funded capability. The analysis identifies specific institutional remedies for licensing, service continuity, procurement oversight, and collective action.
entries.detailTitle: Small States and the Governance of Strategic Space Dependence
keyContributions: Built a structured comparison around specific public functions and the decisions needed to perform them. Examined external dependencies, legal and operational rights, domestic capability, and documented outcomes to assess whether retained authority could support an actual public decision.

Identified distinct mechanisms in the three cases: retained launch-permission authority in New Zealand, operational capability through divided responsibilities in Norway, and the planning and legislative information required alongside asset ownership in Luxembourg.

Proposed an accountable-acceptance standard requiring decision makers to identify who can interrupt essential services, which information and rights permit a response, and what funded capacity enables action. Material gaps would require reasoned acceptance or revision before commitment.

Translated the standard into proposed licensing and procurement terms covering operator information, significant changes, suspension, recovery, and service transition. Connected these terms to lifetime costs, technical staffing, and timely legislative scrutiny of financial commitments.

Analyzed collective agency through anti-satellite-testing commitments, UN consensus procedures, and ESA programme and voting rules. Distinguished participation rights, influence, and implementation capacity, connecting national safeguards to collective restraint on debris and cross-border service disruption.

entries.organization: Who May Choose the Lesser Risk: Solar Geoengineering and the Legal Duties of Comparison and Continuity
entries.summary: Developed two proposed legal duties for solar geoengineering: comparative justification and continuity. Connected risk-risk analysis to authorization by requiring proponents to defend policy alternatives and answer challenges from affected constituencies. Traced termination risk to a separation between political control, operator succession, and the physical cooling trajectory. The resulting framework specifies conditions for deployment and withdrawal, supports governed research, and requires continuing assessment of both intervention and nondeployment.
entries.detailTitle: Who May Choose the Lesser Risk: Solar Geoengineering and the Legal Duties of Comparison and Continuity
keyContributions: Separated historical climate conditions, a future without stratospheric aerosol injection, and feasible policy portfolios as distinct comparators. Analyzed how baseline selection, welfare measures, and distributional assumptions shape the case for intervention and the burdens assigned to exposed populations.

Proposed a comparative justification duty requiring proponents to defend alternatives, disclose distributional choices, and answer substantiated objections. Designed powers for independently selected representatives of exposed constituencies to demand redesign or withhold collective approval.

Developed a continuity duty separating programme control, operator choice, and the cooling trajectory. Specified bounded interim succession, independent monitoring, transition finance, and gradual withdrawal so that political authority can change without automatically triggering abrupt physical cessation.

Mapped environmental assessment, notification, and consultation requirements onto the authorization problem. Distinguished limited research from climate-affecting deployment and proposed scrutiny based on expected effects and cumulative scale, including review of related projects together.

Formulated a proposed priority rule for serious threats to subsistence and survival, requiring comparison of feasible alternatives, shared authorization, and credible relief. Built periodic reassessment of forgone benefits and harms of nondeployment into the same decision process.

entries.organization: Mangrove Restoration and the Limits of Compensatory Mitigation: Lessons from Florida for the Greater Bay Area
entries.summary: Developed a comparative legal framework for deciding when ecological restoration can justify new habitat loss. Distinguished protection, repair, and compensatory mitigation across Florida and the Greater Bay Area, using West Lake, Deep Bay, and San Tin to examine evidence of functional replacement. Proposed site-specific baselines, staged authorization and ecological acceptance, funded correction, and continuing responsibility. The framework connects restoration evidence to development permissions, funding decisions, and the point at which obligations can be discharged.
entries.detailTitle: Mangrove Restoration and the Limits of Compensatory Mitigation: Lessons from Florida for the Greater Bay Area
keyContributions: Organized the legal comparison around habitat protection, repair, and compensation for new loss. Traced duties, approval instruments, and administrative powers across Florida, mainland China, Shenzhen, Hong Kong, and Macao to identify how restoration conditions can take legal effect.

Used West Lake to examine hydrological rehabilitation and Deep Bay and San Tin to assess functional replacement. Distinguished canopy growth, construction, and predicted enhancement from evidence supporting compensation, including additionality and the timing of replacement functions.

Proposed staged approval and acceptance separating engineering completion from ecological performance. Specified site baselines, functional objectives, monitoring periods, seasonal coverage, and review authority, linking damaging development phases to the availability of the functions used to justify them.

Designed proposed arrangements for delayed or failed recovery through funded monitoring, correction, and continuing management. Distinguished contractor performance from ecological uncertainty, and examined retention, financial security, and public budget commitments as instruments for sustaining corrective work.

Linked ecological evidence to fund release, discharge of responsibility, and development permission. Proposed smaller footprints, revised sequencing, alternative sites, or refusal to credit compensation where promised functions lack credible replacement, while allowing proportionate trials in degraded habitats.
